name: Tanh–sinh quadrature
definition: For finite a<b, set c=(a+b)/2, d=(b−a)/2, x(t)=tanh((π/2)sinh t), w(t)=(π/2)cosh(t)/cosh²((π/2)sinh t). Set Q(h,N)=dh Σ_(k=−N)^N f(c+d x(kh))w(kh), approximating ∫_a^b f(s)ds.
variables: a,b interval endpoints; h>0 mesh spacing; N nonnegative integer truncation; c midpoint; d half-width; w derivative of x
assumptions: Integrable f with finite interior samples and a sufficiently smooth, rapidly decaying transformed integrand for useful convergence; rapid double-exponential convergence is conditional
limitations: Endpoint rounding, overflow, cancellation and insufficient tail resolution can corrupt the result; refinement differences are indicators, not certified bounds
failure_conditions: Nonfinite terms or unrepresentable interior nodes
Unresolved tail or mesh refinement within a finite evaluation budget
computation: For fixed h extend N and monitor changes over outer shells; separately halve h while retaining at least the previous transformed extent and rechecking tails. Compare resolved estimates against allocated positive tolerances. Report unresolved convergence on budget exhaustion; a single small tail term is not a certificate. Use stable endpoint complements or higher precision where necessary.

source.citation: Mori, M. (2005), Discovery of the Double Exponential Transformation and Its Developments, Publ. RIMS 41, 897–935, publisher abstract, https://ems.press/journals/prims/articles/2317 ; Boost.Math 1.71 tanh_sinh and 1.66 endpoint handling documentation, https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_71_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/double_exponential/de_tanh_sinh.html ; https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_66_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/double_exponential/de_tanh_sinh_2_arg.html

required_inputs: Integrand, finite interval, positive mesh, truncation and refinement budgets, positive tail and refinement tolerances
mechanism_note: Nonlinear transformation creates clustered nonuniform physical nodes and Jacobian weights; distinct from finite uniform-grid trapezoid, although it uses trapezoidal summation in transformed coordinates.

name: Adaptive Simpson quadrature
definition: S(l,r)=(r−l)[f(l)+4f((l+r)/2)+f(r)]/6; m=(l+r)/2; S₂=S(l,m)+S(m,r); E=|S₂−S(l,r)|/15. If E≤τ, accept S₂+(S₂−S(l,r))/15; otherwise recurse on both halves with local tolerance τ/2 and sum their accepted estimates.
variables: l,r panel endpoints; S coarse estimate; S₂ two-panel estimate; E estimated error of S₂; τ positive local absolute tolerance
assumptions: Finite a<b and finite sampled values; sufficiently smooth integrand with locally stable fourth derivative for asymptotic error scaling; positive tolerance and finite recursion budget
limitations: Estimator can miss localized or oscillatory structure and is not a rigorous bound; correction relies on the same asymptotic scaling
failure_conditions: Nonfinite samples or midpoint indistinguishable from an endpoint
Unresolved estimated error at recursion or evaluation limit
computation: Start on [a,b] with absolute tolerance ε; cache shared samples, bisect as specified and halve the local budget on each child. Sum corrected accepted estimates and record the sum of local indicators; report failure rather than unconditional success if a budget is exhausted.

source.citation: Per-Olof Persson, UC Berkeley Math 128A, Numerical Differentiation and Integration, §4.6 Adaptive Quadrature Methods, https://persson.berkeley.edu/math128a/lecture_notes/math128a_lecture_notes_chapter_4.html ; signed Richardson correction derived from stated 1/16 error scaling.

required_inputs: Integrand, finite interval, positive absolute tolerance, recursion and evaluation limits
incompatible_methods: Treating error estimate as a certificate
mechanism_note: Adaptive subdivision and Richardson correction of composite Simpson; a variant, not an independent algorithm. Unlike Romberg, refinement is local; unlike Gauss–Kronrod, uses Simpson panels.
